summary.big_en: The circulatory system carries food and oxygen to every part of the body and takes waste away.

glossary.def: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood working together to move blood round the body.
glossary.example: Its three main parts are the heart, the blood vessels and the blood (p.3).

glossary.def: The organ that pumps blood around the body.
glossary.example: The left side pumps blood with oxygen to the body; the right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs (p.4).

glossary.def: The movement of blood round the body along the same pathway again and again.
glossary.example: Blood always moves along the same pathway in the blood vessels (p.5).

glossary.def: The red liquid that flows around the body carrying food and oxygen.
glossary.example: Blood carries food particles and oxygen to all parts of the body (p.4).

glossary.def: The tubes that blood moves through.
glossary.example: There are three kinds: arteries, veins and capillaries (p.4).

glossary.def: The gas the body needs to stay alive.
glossary.example: The heart pumps blood in arteries to the lungs to pick up oxygen (p.5).

glossary.def: A waste gas that the body must get rid of.
glossary.example: Blood picks it up from the body and carries it to the lungs (p.4).

glossary.def: The small beat you can feel under the skin, caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it.
glossary.example: Two good places to feel it are the neck and the inside of the wrist (p.7).

glossary.def: The push of the blood against the walls of a blood vessel.
glossary.example: The pressure of the blood is what makes your pulse (p.7).

points.t: The circulatory system has three main parts: the heart, the blood vessels and the blood (p.3).
The heart has two sides. The left side pumps blood with oxygen to the body; the right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs (p.4).
Blood carries food and oxygen to the body, and picks up waste such as carbon dioxide (p.4).
The kidneys and the lungs are the organs that get rid of waste products (p.4).
Blood always travels the same pathway: heart to lungs, back to the heart, out to the body, back again (p.5).
Your heart beats about 90 times a minute now, and about 70 times a minute when you are grown up (p.7).
The more active you are, the more often the heart beats, because the body needs more food and oxygen (p.7).

checklists.title: Three kinds of blood vessel (p.4)

items.look_for: carry blood away from the heart
carry blood back to the heart
join arteries and veins; very narrow with thin walls (p.5)

checklists.note: The only veins that carry blood with oxygen are the ones from the lungs to the heart (p.5).

rows.b: The pressure of blood under the skin
At the neck or the wrist

experiments.title: The pathway of blood
experiments.summary: Follow the drawing of the body: blood without oxygen goes to the lungs, and blood carrying oxygen comes back and is pumped out to the rest of the body.
experiments.result: You can see which vessels carry blood with oxygen and which carry blood without it.

experiments.title: Inside the three blood vessels
experiments.summary: Compare the drawings of an artery, a vein and the capillaries that join them.
experiments.result: An artery has a thick elastic muscular wall, a vein a thin one, and the capillaries are very narrow with thin walls.

experiments.title: Measuring pulse rate
experiments.summary: Find your pulse at the wrist or the neck and count the beats in one minute, three times over, then compare with the rest of the class.
experiments.result: The three counts are not exactly the same, and different people in the class get different rates.

summary.big_en: The respiratory system takes oxygen into the blood and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

glossary.def: The two organs in the chest that fill with air when you breathe in.
glossary.example: They are like stretchy sponges and are protected by the ribs (p.13).

glossary.def: The air tube that leads from the mouth and nose down to the lungs.
glossary.example: Air from the lungs moves up the windpipe when you breathe out (p.14).

glossary.def: The muscle below the lungs that moves to pull air in and push it out.
glossary.example: It relaxes and moves upwards when you breathe out (p.14).

glossary.def: Moving air in and out of the lungs.
glossary.example: We need to breathe to stay alive (p.13).

glossary.def: How many times you breathe in and out in a minute.
glossary.example: Measured by counting breaths over a set time (p.12).

points.t: We use our lungs for breathing, and we need to breathe to stay alive (p.13).
The ribs protect the lungs, which fill with air like stretchy sponges (p.13).
Breathing in moves oxygen from the air into the blood vessels in the lungs (p.14).
As the body uses up oxygen it makes carbon dioxide, which the blood carries back to the lungs to be breathed out (p.14).
Breathing in makes the chest bigger; breathing out makes it smaller and pushes the air out (p.14).

items.look_for: in the chest, protected by the ribs
from the mouth and nose to the lungs

rows.b: Gets smaller, air is pushed out

experiments.title: Breathing in and breathing out
experiments.summary: Compare the two drawings of the chest, one while breathing in and one while breathing out.
experiments.result: Breathing in the ribs move up and out and the diaphragm moves down; breathing out they move the other way.

experiments.title: Investigate breathing
experiments.summary: Put your hands on your rib cage and breathe in and out, then breathe out into a balloon.
experiments.result: The rib cage rises and falls under your hands, and the balloon fills with the air from your lungs.

summary.big_en: Puberty is the stage of life when the body changes so that it will be able to reproduce.

glossary.def: The stage of life when the body changes and becomes able to reproduce.
glossary.example: It usually starts about age 13 in boys and from about age 11 in girls (p.20).

glossary.def: Chemicals made in the body that cause the changes of puberty.
glossary.example: The changes of puberty are caused by hormones (p.20).

glossary.def: The parts of the body used in reproduction.
glossary.example: Boys and girls have different reproductive systems (p.22).

glossary.def: The sex cell made by the male reproductive system.
glossary.example: A sperm joins with an ovum at fertilisation (p.22).

glossary.def: The sex cells made by the female reproductive system; one of them is an ovum.
glossary.example: Ova are released from the ovaries (p.23).

glossary.def: When a sperm and an ovum join together.
glossary.example: Fertilisation is the start of a new living thing (p.23).

glossary.def: The monthly loss of blood from the womb when an ovum is not fertilised.
glossary.example: Menstruation begins during puberty in girls (p.23).

points.t: Puberty does not happen all at once but in stages, and it starts at different ages in boys and girls (p.20).
The first change is a fast growth spurt: boys can grow 10 cm in a year, girls up to 12 cm (p.20).
Both boys and girls grow more body hair and may get oily skin and pimples (p.20).
The changes of puberty are not the same for everyone and do not all happen at the same time (p.20).
Reproduction is part of the life cycle of all living things (p.19).

items.look_for: boys 10 cm, girls up to 12 cm in a year
on the face and armpits in boys; in the armpits in girls
many boys and girls get pimples
broader shoulders and chest, deeper voice
wider hips, breasts develop, voice a little deeper

summary.big_en: Diseases are caused by living things that infect the body. Our defences and good hygiene help keep them out.

glossary.def: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing.
glossary.example: The fungus that causes ringworm is a parasite (p.25).

glossary.def: The living thing that a parasite infects.
glossary.example: A person with malaria is the host of the parasite (p.25).

glossary.def: A way the body stops itself from being infected.
glossary.example: Skin, acid, mucus and tears are the body's defences (p.26).

glossary.def: Something that blocks the way in.
glossary.example: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

glossary.def: Sticky liquid in the nose and air passages that traps germs.
glossary.example: Mucus in the windpipe traps germs before they reach the lungs (p.26).

glossary.def: Keeping yourself and the things around you clean.
glossary.example: Washing hands with soap and water before eating is good hygiene (p.27).

glossary.def: An animal that spreads a disease without getting the disease itself.
glossary.example: Mosquitoes are the vector for malaria (p.29).

glossary.def: Something you put on your skin to keep insects away.
glossary.example: Insect repellents help prevent bites (p.29).

points.t: Diseases stop our bodies from working properly. The living things that cause them grow and reproduce in or on the body (p.25).
Bacteria can only be seen with a microscope, and not all of them are harmful (p.25).
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria, and all viruses are harmful (p.25).
Some fungi are useful, such as the yeast in bread, but others are parasites that cause disease (p.25).
Diseases spread by body contact and in food, water and air (p.27).
An insect vector does not cause the disease and does not get it; it passes on the parasite when it bites (p.29).
The body has its own defences that stop germs getting in and kill the ones that do (p.26).

items.look_for: a barrier that stops germs getting in
stomach acid kills germs in food
traps germs in the nose and air passages
contain a chemical that kills some bacteria

items.sign: Wear long sleeves and long trousers
Close doors and windows at night
Use insect repellent on the skin

experiments.title: Where the body's defences are
experiments.summary: Look at the drawing showing where each of the body's defences works.
experiments.result: Tears at the eyes, mucus in the nose and windpipe, skin over the whole body, and acid in the stomach.

experiments.title: Analyse hygiene methods that people use
experiments.summary: A class surveyed people locally to find out which hygiene methods they use, then drew a dot plot of the results.
experiments.result: Keeping the kitchen, toilet and surroundings clean was used by 12 people, the most of any method; washing hands after working with food was used by 4, the fewest.

summary.big_en: Each substance has its own melting point and boiling point — that is how we tell substances apart.

glossary.def: Something about a substance that allows us to tell it apart from other substances.
glossary.example: Each substance has its own melting point (p.36).

glossary.def: The temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid.
glossary.example: Ice melts at 0 °C; the melting point of gold is 1064 °C (p.36).

glossary.def: The temperature at which particles throughout a liquid have enough energy to change to a gas.
glossary.example: Pure water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C (p.36).

glossary.def: When particles on the surface of a liquid change into a gas.
glossary.example: Evaporation can occur at any temperature (p.36).

glossary.def: Everything that takes up space and has mass. Solid, liquid and gas are its three states.
glossary.example: Air is a mixture of gases, and gas is one of the states of matter (p.35, p.39).

points.t: Melting point is a property of a substance, so each substance has its own melting point (p.36).
Boiling point is a property too. Each substance boils at a certain temperature (p.36).
Boiling and evaporation both change a liquid into a gas, but they are not the same process (p.36).
All matter takes up space and has mass. Air is a mixture of gases, so air is matter (p.39).

checklists.title: Melting points in the book (p.36, p.62)
checklists.note: The Check your progress table (p.62) asks you to list these from highest to lowest.

rows.a: All the particles in the liquid
Most liquids boil only when heated

experiments.title: Measure and compare melting points
experiments.summary: The teacher heats three different solids in pans on a hotplate and measures the temperature of each one the moment it melts.
experiments.result: Each solid melts at a different temperature on the thermometer, and the readings go in a table.

experiments.title: Investigate the properties of gases
experiments.summary: Two blown-up balloons are hung from a ruler so they balance, then the tie on one balloon is loosened to let the air out.
experiments.result: When the tie on one balloon is loosened, the balanced ruler tips down on the side of the full balloon.

summary.big_en: Metals let heat and electricity pass through them. Glass and plastic do not.

glossary.def: Heat being transferred from one object to another.
glossary.example: A cold metal teaspoon in a hot cup of tea: the handle feels warm after a while (p.42-43).

glossary.def: A substance or material that conducts heat well.
glossary.example: Metals. Silver is the best conductor of heat (p.43-44).

glossary.def: A substance or material that is able to conduct electricity.
glossary.example: Metals, such as the copper connecting wire in the circuit (p.45).

glossary.def: A material or substance that is not a good conductor of electricity.
glossary.example: Plastic, rubber, glass and most non-metal substances (p.61).

points.t: Metals are good conductors of heat and silver is the best. Non-metals such as glass and plastic are not good conductors of heat (p.44).
How well a substance can conduct heat is a property of the substance. Some substances conduct heat better than others (p.44).
The ability to conduct electricity is a property of materials and substances. Metals conduct electricity (p.45).
Substances that are not good conductors of electricity are called insulators (p.61).

checklists.title: How well substances conduct — the book's table (p.47)
checklists.note: Measured in W/m−K. Question 4 asks you to find the measurements that do not fit the pattern.

experiments.title: Investigate how well different materials conduct heat
experiments.summary: A bead is stuck with petroleum jelly to the top of a metal spoon, a plastic spoon, a glass rod, a pencil and a piece of polystyrene foam, then all of them are stood in hot water.
experiments.result: The beads fall off one after another, and the order shows which material carried the heat fastest.

experiments.title: Investigate how well different substances conduct electricity
experiments.summary: A lamp circuit is set up with two free wire ends, and different substances (copper, steel, aluminium foil, graphite, sugar, water) are placed between the ends in turn.
experiments.result: For each substance the lamp is bright, dim or does not shine, recorded as two ticks, one tick or none.

summary.big_en: Some changes can be undone and some can never be undone.

glossary.def: A change that alters how a substance looks or feels, without turning it into a new substance.
glossary.example: A change of state, such as ice melting into water (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that can be changed back again.
glossary.example: Solid ice to liquid water, and liquid water back to solid ice (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that cannot be reversed.
glossary.example: Burning a match: the wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

glossary.def: The substance that dissolves.
glossary.example: The dissolved salt in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: The substance in which the solute dissolves.
glossary.example: The water in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: Looking the same throughout.
glossary.example: A solution has a uniform appearance, so you cannot see the solute in it (p.52).

glossary.def: How fast something happens.
glossary.example: Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves (p.53).

points.t: A physical change alters how a substance looks or feels. The substance does not change into a new substance (p.50).
A change is reversible when the substance can be changed back to the way it was (p.50).
Irreversible changes cannot be reversed, and some turn one substance into another. That is a chemical change (p.50).
The solute and the solvent together form a solution. Sea water is salty because there is dissolved salt in the water (p.51).
When a solute dissolves, its particles move between the solvent particles and spread evenly. That is why you cannot see the solute afterwards (p.52).
Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves. It spreads the solute particles into the spaces between the solvent particles more quickly (p.53).
In a heated solvent the particles gain energy and move faster, so the solute dissolves faster (p.54).

rows.b: Sometimes — then it is a chemical change

rows.a: Ice melts to water, water freezes to ice
rows.b: A burning match: wood becomes carbon

experiments.title: Getting started: ice cubes in the sun
experiments.summary: Ice cubes are left on a saucer in a warm place for five minutes, then the water is put back in the freezer.
experiments.result: After five minutes in the warm the ice has melted, and back in the freezer it becomes solid again.

experiments.title: Describe dissolving
experiments.summary: Look at the picture of copper sulfate being added to water and describe what happens to it.
experiments.result: The copper sulfate spreads through the water until you can no longer see it in the solution.

experiments.title: Does water temperature affect the rate of dissolving?
experiments.summary: A teaspoon of sugar is stirred into 100 ml of cold water and into 100 ml of hot water, and the time it takes to dissolve is measured for each.
experiments.result: The sugar in the hot water takes less time on the stopwatch than the sugar in the cold water.

summary.big_en: In a chemical reaction, substances react together and form a new substance.

glossary.def: When substances are mixed together, change, and form a new substance.
glossary.example: Vinegar mixed with bicarbonate of soda (p.57).

glossary.def: What substances do when they change together and form a new substance.
glossary.example: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda react together (p.57).

glossary.def: The substances that react together.
glossary.example: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda (p.57).

glossary.def: The new substances that form in a reaction.
glossary.example: The gas that is produced in the jar (p.57-58).

glossary.def: Something we can see that shows a product has formed.
glossary.example: The gas produced when vinegar and bicarbonate of soda react (p.58).

points.t: In a chemical reaction substances react together and form new substances. The substances that react are the reactants and the new ones are the products (p.57).
Sometimes we can see that a product has formed, and that is evidence of the reaction. There are also other ways to tell (p.58).
When clear limewater is mixed with carbon dioxide, the reaction forms a substance called calcium carbonate (p.59).

checklists.title: Three ways to tell a reaction has taken place (p.59 Q1)
checklists.note: Question 1 asks for three ways with an example of each; the topic's investigations show one each.

experiments.title: Identify reactants and products
experiments.summary: A teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda is added to vinegar in a jar and watched for five minutes.
experiments.result: A gas is produced straight away, and after five minutes you look for any other product.

experiments.title: Investigate evidence A — colour change and a new solid
experiments.summary: Iodine solution is added to water and cornstarch is stirred in; in another beaker, air is breathed through a straw into limewater.
experiments.result: Adding cornstarch to the iodine solution changes what you see, and breathing carbon dioxide into the limewater forms a new substance.

experiments.title: Investigate evidence B — temperature change
experiments.summary: Vinegar is poured over a ball of wire wool in a beaker, and the temperature is recorded straight away and again after five minutes.
experiments.result: The thermometer reading after five minutes is different from the reading taken at the start.

flashcards.back_en: How many times you breathe in and out in a minute.
flashcards.example_en: Measured by counting breaths over a set time (p.12).

flashcards.back_en: The stage of life when the body changes and becomes able to reproduce.
flashcards.example_en: It usually starts about age 13 in boys and from about age 11 in girls (p.20).

flashcards.back_en: Chemicals made in the body that cause the changes of puberty.
flashcards.example_en: The changes of puberty are caused by hormones (p.20).

flashcards.back_en: The parts of the body used in reproduction.
flashcards.example_en: Boys and girls have different reproductive systems (p.22).

flashcards.back_en: The sex cell made by the male reproductive system.
flashcards.example_en: A sperm joins with an ovum at fertilisation (p.22).

flashcards.back_en: The sex cells made by the female reproductive system; one of them is an ovum.
flashcards.example_en: Ova are released from the ovaries (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: When a sperm and an ovum join together.
flashcards.example_en: Fertilisation is the start of a new living thing (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: The monthly loss of blood from the womb when an ovum is not fertilised.
flashcards.example_en: Menstruation begins during puberty in girls (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing.
flashcards.example_en: The fungus that causes ringworm is a parasite (p.25).

flashcards.back_en: The living thing that a parasite infects.
flashcards.example_en: A person with malaria is the host of the parasite (p.25).

flashcards.back_en: A way the body stops itself from being infected.
flashcards.example_en: Skin, acid, mucus and tears are the body's defences (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Something that blocks the way in.
flashcards.example_en: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Sticky liquid in the nose and air passages that traps germs.
flashcards.example_en: Mucus in the windpipe traps germs before they reach the lungs (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Keeping yourself and the things around you clean.
flashcards.example_en: Washing hands with soap and water before eating is good hygiene (p.27).

flashcards.back_en: An animal that spreads a disease without getting the disease itself.
flashcards.example_en: Mosquitoes are the vector for malaria (p.29).

flashcards.back_en: Something you put on your skin to keep insects away.
flashcards.example_en: Insect repellents help prevent bites (p.29).

quiz.stem_en: At what temperature does ice melt?
quiz.why_en: Ice melts at 0 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the melting point of gold?
quiz.why_en: Gold melts at 1064 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: From the Check your progress table, which substance has the LOWEST melting point?
quiz.why_en: Candle wax melts at 60 °C, the lowest in the table (p.62).

quiz.stem_en: Why is the melting point of a substance always lower than its boiling point?

choices.en: Because boiling needs less energy than melting
Because solids are hotter than liquids
Because melting only happens in an oven
Because a substance must be a liquid before it can boil

quiz.why_en: A solid melts into a liquid first; the liquid then needs more energy to boil (p.38 Q5).

quiz.stem_en: Pure water boils at 100 °C. At what temperature does vinegar boil?
quiz.why_en: Vinegar boils at 118 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?

choices.en: Boiling happens through the whole liquid; evaporation only at the surface
Boiling can happen at any temperature; evaporation needs heat

quiz.why_en: In boiling, all the particles gain enough energy; in evaporation only surface particles change to gas (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these can happen at any temperature, without heating?
quiz.why_en: Evaporation can occur at any temperature; most liquids boil only when heated (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: You heat 100 ml of water and 100 ml of vinegar on the same hotplate. Which boils first, and why?

choices.en: Vinegar — it has the lower boiling point
Water — it has the lower boiling point

quiz.why_en: Water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C, so water reaches its boiling point first (p.36, p.38).

quiz.stem_en: Two balloons the same size hang from a balanced ruler. You let the air out of one. What happens?

choices.en: The ruler tips towards the full balloon
The ruler tips towards the empty balloon

quiz.why_en: The full balloon still has the mass of its air, so its side goes down (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't we usually feel the air around us?

choices.en: Because we only feel air when it is moving

quiz.why_en: "We can't feel air unless it is moving" (p.39). Air is still matter.

quiz.stem_en: A cold metal teaspoon is put into hot tea. After a while the handle feels warm. What is this called?
quiz.why_en: Heat is transferred along the spoon — conduction (p.42-43).

quiz.stem_en: In which cup will tea stay warm the longest?
quiz.why_en: Polystyrene foam is a poor conductor of heat, so heat stays in the tea (p.45 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: Why does food cook faster in the oven in a metal dish than in a glass dish?

choices.en: Metal dishes are lighter than glass dishes are
Glass reflects the oven heat away from the food
Metal dishes are made bigger than glass ones
Metal conducts heat to the food faster than glass

quiz.why_en: Metal is a good thermal conductor; glass is not (p.62 Q2, p.44).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a non-metal that CAN conduct electricity?
quiz.why_en: Pencil graphite lights the lamp in the circuit test (p.45-46).

quiz.stem_en: Why are plugs and wire coverings made of plastic or rubber?

choices.en: They are electrical insulators, so electricity cannot reach you

quiz.why_en: Plastic and rubber are electrical insulators (p.61).

quiz.stem_en: Ice melts into water, then the water is put back in the freezer. What kind of change is this?
quiz.why_en: Water can change back to ice — a reversible physical change (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: When a match burns, what does the wood change into?
quiz.why_en: The wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: Does boiling an egg cause a reversible or irreversible change?

choices.en: Irreversible — the egg cannot go back to raw

quiz.why_en: A cooked egg is a new substance and cannot be changed back (p.50 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: Sort these: which ONE is an irreversible process?
quiz.why_en: Rusting makes a new substance and cannot be reversed; the others are physical changes (p.62 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: In salty sea water, which is the solute and which is the solvent?

choices.en: Salt is the solvent, water is the solute
Salt is the solute, water is the solvent

quiz.why_en: The substance that dissolves is the solute (salt); it dissolves in the solvent (water) (p.51).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't you see the salt after it dissolves in water?

choices.en: The salt sinks to the bottom out of sight
The salt turns into water and stops existing
The salt particles spread evenly between the water particles
The salt floats on the top as a thin film

quiz.why_en: Solute particles spread evenly among the solvent particles — the solution looks uniform (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: Using the particle model, why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?

choices.en: Heat gives the particles energy so they move faster and spread out
Sugar particles get smaller in heat

quiz.why_en: Heat adds energy; particles move faster and spread the solute through the solvent more easily (p.54).

quiz.stem_en: Will sugar dissolve in a cup of cold water if nobody stirs it?

choices.en: Only if the cup is metal
Yes, but slowly — particles are always moving

quiz.why_en: Particles in matter are always moving, so it dissolves on its own given time (p.54 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: You put vinegar and bicarbonate of soda in a jar. Which are the reactants?
quiz.why_en: The reactants are the substances that react together (p.57).

quiz.stem_en: Your teacher holds a spoon over a burning candle. Which change is a chemical reaction?
quiz.why_en: Melting and hardening wax are reversible; the burning wick forms new substances (p.56).

quiz.stem_en: Limewater mixed with carbon dioxide forms calcium carbonate. Which is the PRODUCT?
quiz.why_en: Calcium carbonate is the new substance formed (p.59 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: You add cornstarch to water with iodine solution and stir. What evidence of a reaction do you see?
quiz.why_en: The colour changes — investigation A (p.58).

quiz.stem_en: You breathe through a straw into limewater. What do you see, and why?

choices.en: It stays clear because nothing at all reacts
It turns cloudy — carbon dioxide in your breath reacts
It turns bright blue because of the oxygen
It bubbles because the straw adds air to it

quiz.why_en: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to make cloudy calcium carbonate (p.58-59).

quiz.stem_en: Zara drops a fizzy tablet into water. What evidence of a chemical reaction will she see?
quiz.why_en: Gas is produced — one of the signs of a reaction (p.59 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: Boiling water makes bubbles too. Why is that NOT a chemical reaction?

choices.en: Because no new substance forms — the water just becomes a gas
Because water bubbles are always too small
Because boiling needs a flame and not a reaction
Because the bubbles rise instead of sinking

quiz.why_en: Evidence means a PRODUCT has formed. Boiling is a change of state, not a new substance (p.58, p.36).

quiz.stem_en: Water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C and olive oil at 300 °C. Heated equally, which turns into a gas first?

choices.en: Olive oil — it is the thickest
Vinegar — it is in the middle
They all turn to gas together
Water — it has the lowest boiling point

quiz.why_en: The liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches it first (WB p.21).

quiz.stem_en: Why is a wooden spoon good for stirring soup cooking in a pot?

choices.en: Wood makes the soup taste better
Wood is a poor conductor, so heat does not travel to your hand
Wood conducts heat faster than metal

quiz.why_en: Non-metals such as wood are not good conductors of heat (p.44, WB p.24).

quiz.stem_en: Iron and sulfur are mixed and form iron sulfide. Which is the product?
quiz.why_en: The new substance that forms is the product (WB p.33).

quiz.stem_en: Cooking gas burns in oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water. Which of these is a reactant?
quiz.why_en: Oxygen is one of the substances that react; carbon dioxide and water are the products (WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: Magnesium is mixed with oxygen: there is a bright white flame and a white powder. Which is the product?
quiz.why_en: The powder is the new substance formed; the flame is evidence, not a product (WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make oxygen and glucose. Which are the reactants?
quiz.why_en: The substances that react together are the reactants (WB p.35).

quiz.stem_en: True or false: gases do not have mass because we cannot see them.

choices.en: True — you cannot weigh a gas
True — only solids and liquids have mass
False — gases have mass only when cold
False — gases have mass even though we cannot see them

quiz.why_en: All matter takes up space and has mass (p.39); the teacher's slide sets this as false (LMS: Week 7 slides).

quiz.stem_en: True or false: evaporation only happens when a liquid reaches its boiling point.

choices.en: False — evaporation can happen at any temperature
True — it needs the boiling point

quiz.why_en: Evaporation can occur at any temperature (p.36); the slide sets this as false (LMS: Week 7 slides).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a property of a substance?
quiz.why_en: A property is something about the substance itself (LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Three substances melt at 25 °C, 80 °C and 150 °C. Which melts first when they are heated together?

choices.en: They all melt at the same time

quiz.why_en: The lowest melting point is reached first (LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a reversible change?
quiz.why_en: Melting can be reversed by freezing; burning and cooking make new substances (p.50, LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Which TWO properties does all matter have?

choices.en: It takes up space and it has mass
It is heavy and it is hot
It can be seen and it can be felt

quiz.why_en: All matter takes up space and has mass — including gases like air (p.39).

quiz.stem_en: Which substance is the best conductor of heat?
quiz.why_en: "Silver is the best conductor of heat" (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: A bead is stuck with petroleum jelly onto a metal spoon, a plastic spoon and a glass rod, and all three are stood in hot water. Why does the bead on the metal spoon fall off first?

choices.en: Metal conducts heat best, so the jelly melts first
The bead was stuck on badly

quiz.why_en: Metal conducts heat fastest, melting the petroleum jelly first (p.43-44).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: copper 386, aluminium 237, graphite 168, brass 150, steel 80. Which conducts heat worst?
quiz.why_en: Steel has the lowest heat value in the table, 80 W/m−K (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting electricity: copper 59, aluminium 37, brass 16, steel 10, graphite 1. Which conducts electricity best?
quiz.why_en: Copper has the highest electricity value, 59 (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: A solution looks the same all the way through. What word describes this?
quiz.why_en: A solution has a uniform appearance (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: Two teaspoons of sugar are put into a cup of coffee, which is then drunk without being stirred. It still tastes bitter. Why?

choices.en: He did not stir, so the sugar had not dissolved

quiz.why_en: Without stirring, the sugar stayed at the bottom (p.53).

quiz.stem_en: Name TWO things that make a solid dissolve faster.

choices.en: Using a bigger jar and more water

quiz.why_en: Stirring and heating both increase the rate of dissolving (p.53-54).

quiz.stem_en: An iron nail is left in a saucer of water. A few days later it has rusted. What is the product of the reaction?
quiz.why_en: The nail had rusted, so rust is the new substance that formed (p.62 Q5).

quiz.stem_en: Vinegar is poured over a ball of wire wool. A reading is taken straight away and again after five minutes. What is being measured?
quiz.why_en: You record the thermometer before and after — a temperature change is evidence (p.59).

quiz.stem_en: How well a substance conducts heat is an example of what?
quiz.why_en: How well a substance can conduct heat is a property of the substance (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: At what temperature does acetone boil?
quiz.why_en: Acetone boils at 50.5 °C (WB p.19).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: silver 420, copper 400, aluminium 250, brass 109, iron 80, stainless steel 15. Which metal conducts heat best?
quiz.why_en: Silver has the highest value, 420 (WB p.24). Note this is a different table from the one on p.47.

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: silver 420, copper 400, aluminium 250, brass 109, iron 80, stainless steel 15. Which metal conducts heat worst?
quiz.why_en: Stainless steel has the lowest value, 15 (WB p.24).

quiz.stem_en: Different lengths of graphite are put in a circuit and the lamp brightness is scored 0–5. A 2 cm piece scores 5 and a 12 cm piece scores 0. What does that show?

choices.en: The longer the graphite, the dimmer the lamp
Graphite is not a conductor at all
Longer graphite makes the lamp brighter

quiz.why_en: Brightness falls as the graphite gets longer in their results table (WB p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar is stirred a few times into a cup of warm tea, and afterwards some sugar is still at the bottom of the cup. What two things would have made it all dissolve?
quiz.why_en: Stirring and a higher temperature both increase the rate of dissolving (p.53-54, WB p.30).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar takes 90 s to dissolve at 20 °C, 40 s at 40 °C, 25 s at 60 °C and 15 s at 80 °C. What is the pattern?

choices.en: The hotter the water, the longer it takes
The hotter the water, the less time the sugar takes

quiz.why_en: Their results show the dissolving time falling as temperature rises (WB p.31).

quiz.stem_en: Heat and electricity values: copper 386 and 59, aluminium 237 and 37, brass 150 and 16, steel 80 and 10, graphite 168 and 1. Which substance does NOT fit the pattern that a good heat conductor is also a good electrical conductor?
quiz.why_en: Graphite conducts heat well (168) but electricity very poorly (1) (p.47 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: A lamp has a metal filament, metal support wires, a metal screw-in base and a glass bulb. Which part is NOT an electrical conductor?
quiz.why_en: Glass is an insulator; the metal parts carry the electricity (WB p.23).

quiz.stem_en: What are the three main parts of the circulatory system?

choices.en: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood
The heart, the lungs and the ribs
The blood, the kidneys and the skin
The lungs, the windpipe and the diaphragm

quiz.why_en: The circulatory system has three main parts (p.3).

quiz.stem_en: Which side of the heart pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs?

choices.en: Neither side, the lungs pump it

quiz.why_en: The right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs only (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Where does the left side of the heart pump blood to?
quiz.why_en: The left side pumps blood that contains oxygen all around the body (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: What are the three kinds of blood vessel?
quiz.why_en: There are three kinds of blood vessels (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which waste gas does the blood carry away from the body?
quiz.why_en: Carbon dioxide is a waste gas that the body must get rid of (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which two organs help the body get rid of waste products?
quiz.why_en: The kidneys and lungs are body organs that help get rid of waste (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which veins are the only ones that carry blood containing oxygen?

choices.en: The veins from the body back to the heart
The veins that go from the heart to the body
The veins from the lungs back to the heart
All veins carry blood with oxygen

quiz.why_en: Those are the only veins that carry blood with oxygen (p.5).

quiz.stem_en: About how many times a minute does a child's heart beat?
quiz.why_en: Your heart beats about 90 times a minute, and about 70 when grown up (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: What causes your pulse?

choices.en: The pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it
The muscles of the arm tightening

quiz.why_en: The pulse is caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: Why does the heart beat more often when you run around?

choices.en: The blood gets thicker when you run
The body needs more food and oxygen
The lungs get smaller when you run
The heart muscle gets tired and slows

quiz.why_en: The more active you are, the more often the heart must beat (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: Which three things make up the respiratory system?

choices.en: Two lungs, the heart, and blood vessels
The nose, the stomach, and the ribs
Two lungs, air tubes, and muscles in the chest
The windpipe, the kidneys, and the diaphragm

quiz.why_en: The human respiratory system contains these parts (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What protects the lungs?
quiz.why_en: The lungs are in the chest and are protected by the ribs (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: When you breathe in, where does the oxygen go?

choices.en: Into the blood vessels in the lungs
Into the windpipe and stays there
Into the muscles of the chest

quiz.why_en: Oxygen gas from the air moves into the blood vessels in the lungs (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: Where does the carbon dioxide in your breath come from?

choices.en: It comes in from the air you breathe
The body makes it as it uses up oxygen
The lungs make it out of water
The heart makes it from food

quiz.why_en: As your body uses up oxygen, it makes carbon dioxide (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: When you breathe out, what do the ribs and the diaphragm do?

choices.en: The ribs move up and out; the diaphragm moves down
Both the ribs and the diaphragm move down
The ribs move down and in; the diaphragm relaxes and moves up
The ribs stay still; only the diaphragm moves down

quiz.why_en: That is how the chest gets smaller and air is pushed out (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: What is the stage of life called when the body becomes able to reproduce?
quiz.why_en: This stage in your life is called puberty (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: What causes the changes that happen during puberty?

choices.en: Chemicals in the body called hormones

quiz.why_en: These changes are caused by hormones (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: At about what age does puberty usually start in boys?
quiz.why_en: In boys, puberty usually starts at about 13 (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: How much can girls grow in a year as puberty starts?
quiz.why_en: Girls can grow up to 12 cm in a year; boys can easily grow 10 cm (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: What is fertilisation?

choices.en: When a sperm and an ovum join together

quiz.why_en: Fertilisation is when a sperm joins with an ovum (p.23).

quiz.stem_en: What is a parasite?

choices.en: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing
Any living thing that is too small to see
Any germ that lives in water

quiz.why_en: That is the definition the book gives (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: What do we call the living thing that a parasite infects?
quiz.why_en: The living thing that a parasite infects is called the host (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Which statement about bacteria and viruses is correct?

choices.en: All bacteria are harmful, but not all viruses are
All viruses are harmful, but not all bacteria are

quiz.why_en: Not all bacteria are harmful; all viruses are harmful (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these diseases is caused by a fungus?
quiz.why_en: Ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by fungi (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Yeast used to make bread rise is a fungus. What does that show?

choices.en: Not every fungus is a parasite that causes disease
Bread can give you a disease
All fungi are useful to people
Yeast is really a kind of bacteria

quiz.why_en: Some fungi are useful, but some are parasites that cause disease (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: How does the skin defend the body against disease?

choices.en: It traps germs in sticky mucus
It acts as a barrier that stops germs getting in
It kills germs with a chemical in tears
It kills germs with stomach acid

quiz.why_en: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: What does the acid in your stomach do?

choices.en: It traps germs in the nose
It kills germs in the food we have eaten
It carries germs to the kidneys

quiz.why_en: Acid in the stomach kills germs in food (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Which defence traps germs in the nose and windpipe?
quiz.why_en: Sticky mucus in the nose and air passages traps germs (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Diseases spread in four ways. Which list is right?

choices.en: Body contact, food, water and air
Body contact, soil, sunlight and air

quiz.why_en: Diseases can be spread by body contact and in food, in water and in the air (p.27).

quiz.stem_en: Mosquitoes spread malaria but do not get the disease. What are they called?
quiz.why_en: We say the insects are vectors (p.29).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these helps prevent a disease that is spread by insects?
quiz.why_en: Sleeping under bed nets is one of the ways to prevent insect bites (p.29).

quiz.stem_en: In a class survey of 38 answers, 12 people kept the kitchen and toilet clean and 4 washed their hands after working with food. What does that show?

choices.en: Washing hands after food was the most popular method by far
Everyone in the survey used exactly the same method
Nobody in the survey covered their nose when sneezing
Keeping surroundings clean was the most used method and washing hands after food the least

quiz.why_en: 12 was the highest count and 4 the lowest in the survey results (p.28).
